--- title: "Data Visualization" description: "Chapter 4: what graphs are for, how people read them, choosing a graph, data visualization with Seaborn and Matplotlib, publication-ready and honest graphs, and exporting figures." format: deck-html execute: echo: false freeze: auto --- # Data Visualization A graph is an instrument and an argument **Chapter 4** Polla Fattah --- ## By the end of today you can - explain why graphs are needed alongside numerical summaries; - tell exploratory graphs from explanatory ones; - explain why position and length are read more accurately than angle, area, or colour; - choose a graph from the question and the variables; - build graphs with Seaborn and Matplotlib from data, visual mappings, and axes; - judge whether a graph is honest, and improve a misleading one; - export figures at the size and resolution a thesis needs. --- ## Summaries can hide almost anything ```python anscombe.groupby("dataset").agg( mean_x=("x", "mean"), mean_y=("y", "mean"), std_y=("y", "std") ) ``` | Dataset | mean x | mean y | std y | correlation | |---|---|---|---|---| | I to IV | 9.0 | 7.5 | 2.03 | 0.82 | Anscombe's four datasets share every numerical summary. --- ## Four identical summaries, four different stories ::: {#59d88cd5 .cell fig-height='3.2' fig-width='9' execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-1.png){width=1410 height=420} ::: ::: A line, a curve, an outlier, and one point making the whole trend. --- ## Look first > **Anyone who analysed these data without looking would draw the same, wrong, conclusion from all four.** Many errors in data, and in reasoning about data, are found only by looking. --- ## Exploring and explaining | | Exploratory graph | Explanatory graph | |---|---|---| | for | the researcher | the reader | | purpose | understand the data | show a known finding | | number | many, quickly | a few, carefully | | polish | none needed | clear message and labels | A thesis contains a few explanatory graphs, chosen from many exploratory ones. --- ## A graph turns numbers into visual properties ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["Position on a
common scale"] --> B["Length"] --> C["Angle
and slope"] --> D["Area"] --> E["Colour
shade"] ``` Cleveland and McGill's experiments: judged most accurately on the left, least on the right. Put the most important comparison into position or length. --- ## The same five numbers, two ways ::: {#1c5cecc7 .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='9' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=1220 height=510} ::: ::: In the pie the slices look equal. In the bars the decline from A to E is obvious. --- ## Two more rules of thumb - put values to be compared **next to each other on the same scale**, within one panel; - use colour to **separate a few categories**, not to carry the main message. Prefer bar charts and dot plots to pie charts, and scatter plots to bubble charts. --- ## Choosing a graph | Question | Variables | Graph | Seaborn tool | |---|---|---|---| | how are values distributed? | one numeric | histogram, KDE | `sns.histplot`, `sns.kdeplot` | | how many in each category? | one categorical | count bar chart | `sns.countplot` | | do groups differ? | numeric by categorical | box plot, strip plot | `sns.boxplot`, `sns.stripplot` | | how are two variables related? | two numeric | scatter, regression | `sns.scatterplot`, `sns.regplot` | | how does it change over time? | numeric over time | line chart | `sns.lineplot` | | how do many variables relate? | several numeric | heat map | `sns.heatmap` | --- ## The anatomy of Python visualization ```{mermaid} flowchart LR D["Data
Pandas DataFrame"] --> S["Seaborn
Statistical abstraction"] --> M["Matplotlib
Axes & Figure control"] ``` Seaborn creates statistical graphics with one concise call, while Matplotlib lets you customize titles, limits, and annotations. --- ## Figure and Axes give the canvas :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ```python pilot = pd.DataFrame({ "sleep": [6.5, 7.5, 5.5, 8.0, 6.0], "stress": [3.2, 2.1, 4.5, 1.8, 3.9] }) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5)) ax.set_xlabel("Sleep (hours)") ax.set_ylabel("Stress (1 to 5)") plt.show() ``` The axes exist, but nothing is drawn yet. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#f604b102 .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='4.3' execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=616 height=481} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Seaborn draws the data onto the axes :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ```python fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5)) sns.scatterplot( data=pilot, x="sleep", y="stress", s=80, color="#1d588c", ax=ax ) plt.show() ``` One point per row. Passing `ax=ax` connects Seaborn directly to the Matplotlib canvas. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#5d0cb36f .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='4.3' execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=616 height=481} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## One row per student ```python first_sem = ( semesters[semesters["semester"] == 1] .merge(students, on="student_id") ) ``` Each student's first-semester record, with their background information. Most graphs are simplest with one row per case. --- ## Histograms show a distribution :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ```python fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5)) sns.histplot( data=first_sem, x="sleep_hours", binwidth=0.5, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white", ax=ax ) ``` Bell-shaped, centred a little above 6 hours. `r round(100 * (first_sem['sleep_hours'] < 7).mean())`% of students sleep less than the recommended 7. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#6142cee2 .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='4.3' execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=616 height=481} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## The binwidth changes the picture ::: {#4b688b8c .cell fig-height='3.2' fig-width='9' execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=1320 height=451} ::: ::: Too narrow is noisy, too wide hides the shape. Try a few widths. --- ## Count charts count categories :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ```python fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5)) sns.countplot( data=students, y="faculty", color="#1d588c", ax=ax ) ``` `sns.countplot()` counts rows automatically. For precomputed values such as averages, use `sns.barplot()`. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#4e746b76 .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='4.3' execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=613 height=481} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Box plots compare groups :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ```python fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5)) sns.boxplot( data=first_sem, x="study_mode", y="wellbeing", color="#eaf0f7", ax=ax ) ``` Part-time students sit a little lower, but the boxes overlap considerably. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#ccd80d98 .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='4.3' execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=615 height=480} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Reading a box plot | Part | Shows | |---|---| | box | the interquartile range (IQR, middle 50%) | | line inside | the median | | whiskers | typical range ($1.5 \times \text{IQR}$) | | points beyond | outliers / extreme values | Whether the study-mode difference is larger than chance is a question for Chapter 8. --- ## Scatter plots show relationships :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ```python fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5)) sns.regplot( data=first_sem, x="sleep_hours", y="gpa", scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.35, "color": "#1d588c"}, line_kws={"color": "#b4762e"}, ax=ax ) ``` `alpha` makes points transparent against **overplotting**. The line rises gently, but points scatter widely. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#f9c6f94c .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='4.3' execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=616 height=481} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Line charts show change over time :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ```python fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5)) sns.lineplot( data=wellbeing_by_sem, x="semester", y="wellbeing", hue="workshop", marker="o", palette=["#1d588c", "#b4762e"], ax=ax ) ``` Shows the longitudinal trajectory across all four study periods. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#511c1237 .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='4.3' execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=615 height=481} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Mapping (`hue`) vs Setting (`color`) ```python sns.lineplot(data=df, x="x", y="y", hue="group") # mapped: color varies by group sns.histplot(data=df, x="x", color="steelblue") # set: one fixed color everywhere ``` | | Data Mapping (`hue`) | Fixed Styling (`color`) | |---|---|---| | meaning | depends on variable values | uniform for the entire plot | | legend | created automatically | no redundant legend | --- ## A common visualization mistake :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ```python # Unnecessary mapping for one constant sns.barplot( data=faculty_means, x="faculty", y="wellbeing", hue="faculty" # redundant! ) ``` Using `hue` for categorical variables already labeled on the axis creates visual clutter and a useless legend. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#cc83f33b .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='4.3' execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=614 height=479} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## From exploratory to explanatory ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["Descriptive Labels"] --> B["Honest Scales"] --> C["Accessible Palettes"] --> D["Targeted Annotations"] ``` Each addition is a purposeful design decision to aid reader comprehension. --- ## Clear labels with measurement units ```python fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4)) sns.lineplot( data=wellbeing_by_sem, x="semester", y="wellbeing", hue="workshop", marker="o", ax=ax ) ax.set_title("Student Wellbeing Trajectory Over Two Years", fontsize=13, weight="bold") ax.set_xlabel("Semester (Measurement Wave)", fontsize=11) ax.set_ylabel("Mean Wellbeing Score (0 to 100)", fontsize=11) ``` Always include the scale range or physical units in parentheses. --- ## Colour-blind-friendly palettes - **Qualitative**: `palette="tab10"` or `palette="Set2"` for unordered groups. - **Sequential**: `palette="viridis"` or `palette="Blues"` for numeric quantities. - **Diverging**: `palette="vlag"` or `palette="coolwarm"` centered on a neutral midpoint. Roughly 8% of men and 0.5% of women have color vision deficiency; avoid rainbow/jet palettes. --- ## Annotations give immediate reference :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ```python fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5)) sns.histplot(data=first_sem, x="sleep_hours", binwidth=0.5, ax=ax) ax.axvline(7, color="darkred", linestyle="--") ax.text(7.1, 75, "Recommended: 7h", color="darkred") ``` Guides the eye directly to the clinical or theoretical threshold. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#3a86e6fa .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='4.3' execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=616 height=481} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## A graph can be accurate and still mislead Most misleading graphs are not deliberate fraud—they arise from unexamined software defaults. | Design Choice | Research Risk | |---|---| | Truncated bar axis | Bar lengths exaggerate minute group differences | | Squashed aspect ratio | Artificially steepens or flattens trends | | 3D effects / Clutter | Distorts perspective and distracts from data | | Rainbow palettes | False boundaries created by perceptual non-uniformity | --- ## Bar axes must start at zero A bar represents quantity through **physical length** from the baseline. If the axis is truncated, a bar twice as tall no longer indicates twice as much value. Points, lines, and dot plots represent quantity through **position**, allowing zoomed views if clearly noted in the caption. --- ## A misleading graph: truncated baseline ::: {#f997423a .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='9' execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=1320 height=481} ::: ::: Education appears several times taller than Social Sciences, yet actual averages differ by only 3 points out of 100! --- ## The same data, redesigned honestly ::: {#b540301e .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='9' execution_count=15} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-16-output-1.png){width=1339 height=481} ::: ::: Differences between faculties are negligible compared to the substantial variation among individual students. --- ## Facets: small multiples :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ```python g = sns.FacetGrid( first_sem, col="programme", col_wrap=3, height=2.8 ) g.map_dataframe( sns.scatterplot, x="sleep_hours", y="gpa", alpha=0.4 ) ``` Identical shared axes enable rapid, accurate visual comparisons. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#618d942b .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='4.5' execution_count=16} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-17-output-1.png){width=634 height=226} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Density plots compare whole distributions :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ```python sem2 = ( semesters[semesters["semester"] == 2] .merge(students, on="student_id") ) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5)) sns.kdeplot( data=sem2, x="wellbeing", hue="workshop", fill=True, alpha=0.3, palette=[navy, copper], ax=ax ) ``` Shows that the entire distribution shifted upward, not just a handful of students. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#b01f656e .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='4.3' execution_count=17} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-18-output-1.png){width=615 height=481} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Correlation heatmaps ::: {#4a9d851a .cell fig-height='4' fig-width='6.5' execution_count=18} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-19-output-1.png){width=726 height=569} ::: ::: A diverging palette centered at 0 with overlaid numeric coefficients prevents misreading subtle color tints. --- ## Exporting publication-ready figures ```python # High-resolution raster for thesis drafts fig.savefig("figures/wellbeing.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight") # Scalable vector graphics for final submission fig.savefig("figures/wellbeing.pdf", bbox_inches="tight") ``` | Decision | Recommended Practice | |---|---| | Width | 8 cm (single-column) or 16 cm (full page width) | | Resolution | At least 300 DPI for raster formats | | Format | PDF or SVG for publication; PNG for web / slides | | Font size | Minimum 9–10 pt when rendered at final physical dimensions | --- ## Practical lab: the Chapter 4 playground Work through the interactive Pyodide exercises in your browser, complete with hints and solutions: - **A. Practise the chapter**: Histograms, ordered count plots, box plots, scatter regression, and zero-baseline redesigns. - **B. Go further**: Dot plots, longitudinal scales, Anscombe's quartet, jittered regressions. - **C. Check your understanding**: Core conceptual questions. - **D. Do it yourself**: Open-ended thesis visualization tasks. All exercises also run locally in VS Code with the downloadable `chapter04.zip`. --- ## Completion checklist - [ ] Every variable was visually inspected prior to formal inferential testing; - [ ] Plot type matches the research question and variable measurement levels; - [ ] The primary comparison is encoded using position or length; - [ ] Axes include descriptive variable titles and measurement units; - [ ] Bar charts strictly start at zero baseline; - [ ] Color palettes are accessible, color-blind friendly, and non-redundant; - [ ] Visualizations are saved at reproduction dimensions with `bbox_inches="tight"`. --- ## The chapter in one sentence > **Inspect the distribution of your data first, then choose a visualization that encodes key comparisons into position or length while honestly conveying magnitude.** --- ## Next: Chapter 5 Moving from data collection to rigorous scientific enquiry: - Moving from a topic to a testable research question and operational hypothesis; - Constructs, measurement levels, reliability, and validity; - Observational vs experimental study designs; - Pre-registration and an analysis plan established before data inspection. --- ## Questions & Discussion Think of a published graph that influenced your thinking. Would its conclusion remain compelling if the vertical axis were reset to its theoretical baseline?
